title: Blinded Self-Trials for Your Supplement Stack
one_liner: Mail-order double-blind crossover kits that tell you which of your own supplements move your own labs and wearable data, and which you can stop paying for.
customer: Adults 35-65 spending $60-300 per month on vitamins, longevity stacks and nootropics. About 8 in 10 Americans take supplements, per a Pew survey published in September 2026. First reached through biohacker communities and health podcasts; later through functional-medicine and longevity practitioners who want evidence for their patients.
problem: Nobody knows whether magnesium, ashwagandha, creatine, NMN or fish oil does anything for them. Population trials show small average effects, but individual responders exist, and without blinding the placebo effect swamps everything. People keep stacks running indefinitely out of subscription inertia and spend hundreds to thousands of dollars per year with no feedback loop.
solution: The customer sends the product they already take. A partner packer or compounding pharmacist repackages it and a matched placebo into coded weekly pouches on a randomized ABAB crossover schedule with washout. Outcomes are chosen per compound: sleep and HRV from the customer's own wearable, glucose from an over-the-counter CGM (Stelo or Lingo), and fingerstick or lab draws for ApoB, hs-CRP, ferritin or vitamin D. Pre-registered Bayesian analysis returns 'keep, drop or inconclusive' with the confidence. Offered for supplements only (never prescription drugs), as self-experimentation, not medical advice. An annual 'Stack Audit' rotates one compound every six weeks.
why_now: Over-the-counter CGMs and consumer wearables now supply continuous, cheap outcome data for healthy people; fingerstick lab kits and direct-to-consumer lab ordering are cheap; supplement use is near-universal and skepticism is rising in coverage of 'mostly useless' supplements; and longevity stack culture gives buyers a natural stack to audit.
revenue_model: $129-199 per compound trial plus lab costs at cost; $349 per year Stack Audit; $60 per patient white-label for practitioners; aggregated, consented responder data licensed to academic researchers (never sold to supplement brands, to protect independence).
non_obvious_insight: The most valuable longevity product for the middle class is subtraction. The average effect of most supplements is tiny but individuals differ, and 'proven for me' is the only evidence class people trust. Unlike the industry, this business makes money when people buy less: every dropped supplement saves $20-40 per month, so the service pays for itself in months and the buyer's own spending is the marketing.
first_30_days: Recruit 40 volunteers from biohacking and supplement communities for a $49 pilot on two popular compounds (for example magnesium glycinate for sleep and creatine for energy). Have a local compounding pharmacist or contract packer prepare coded pouches and placebo. Pre-register the analysis in a public spreadsheet, run the trial, and publish an honest 'what we found, including nulls' post. Pitch five functional-medicine practices on white-labeling the kits at $60 per patient.

title: Sole-source price-reasonableness memos from council agenda data
one_liner: A buy-side benchmark built from public council packets showing what other governments pay Tyler, Axon, OpenGov and Flock, sold as the missing price-reasonableness memo for every sole-source renewal.
customer: Finance directors, IT directors, purchasing officers and clerks in cities and counties of 5k-250k renewing proprietary software (ERP, permitting, body cameras, ALPR). They pay $495-$1,500 per renewal brief or $3k/year subscription. Councilmembers who want a sanity check are the second audience.
problem: Vendors keep pricing confidential, and sole-source renewals sail through with no comparison. Steuben County, NY approved a five-year Tyler MUNIS/Enterprise renewal at $287,644 in 2026/27 rising 5% a year to $349,633, and the record shows no benchmarking or alternatives (5-0 vote, July 14, 2026). Danbury, CT renewed OpenGov ($71,490.65) and Tyler MUNIS ($299,274.89) unanimously as sole-source because each vendor 'is the developer of proprietary systems' (Aug 5, 2026). In National City, CA a councilmember balked at a $250,000 Tyler budgeting module ('It is a $250,000'), the public questioned the sole-source, and the council demanded a white paper with precise terms and fees.
solution: Continuously ingest agenda packets from the big agenda platforms (Legistar, Granicus, CivicClerk, CivicPlus AgendaCenter) and use LLM extraction to build a structured contract table: vendor, product, price, term, escalator, termination clause, and normalized unit metrics (per capita, per seat, per officer, per camera). Anyone facing a renewal enters the vendor and product and gets a one-page brief within a day. It gives the comparable set, the median escalator, the clauses other governments got (price caps, termination for convenience, data-export rights) and a draft sole-source price-reasonableness paragraph the purchasing officer can attach to the staff report. Later: optional negotiation support on success fee.
why_now: Multi-year Tyler and other vendor contracts are coming up for renewal in 2026, and budgets are squeezed by federal cost shifts (SNAP admin share rising to 75% in October 2026) and grant uncertainty. Agenda packets are now machine-readable at scale. Cheap LLM extraction turns a decade of scattered PDFs into a price table, which was not economically possible before.
revenue_model: $495-1,500 per renewal brief; $3k/year unlimited briefs for a county; 15% of first-year savings for negotiated renewals. Secondary revenue: a quarterly 'what governments pay' index for councils and state associations of counties.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce item is not the data, it is a price-reasonableness determination. Sole-source is only defensible when the buyer can document that the price is reasonable, and none of these records shows one. The public packets already contain the answer, and every vendor claims pricing is confidential while its own contracts are posted in agenda PDFs. Evidence: Steuben County renewal, no alternatives documented (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9150000/new-york/steuben-county/finance-secures-fiveyear-renewal-pricing-for-munisenterprise-erp-committee-approves); Danbury sole-source renewals (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/8951200/connecticut/fairfield/danbury-city/board-renews-opengov-and-tyler-munis-contracts-totaling-roughly-370000); National City council asking for the terms and fees (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/9526083/california/san-diego-county/national-city/council-asks-city-manager-for-white-paper-after-tyler-technologies-budgeting-demo). Elko's five-year Axon extension at about $91,200 a year is another comparable data point (https://citizenportal.ai/articles/7804457/nevada/elko-county/elko-city/elko-approves-five-year-axon-contract-for-body-cameras-and-redaction-software-to-clear-backlog).
first_30_days: Scrape agenda packets from 300 mid-size jurisdictions in 2 states and extract about 500 contracts for 5 vendors. Publish a free 'What governments actually pay Tyler' leaderboard to earn inbound. Identify contracts expiring in 6-9 months from the term dates in old packets and email those finance directors a free sample brief. Sell the first 10 briefs at $495. Get 2 governments to attach the memo to a staff report as a proof point.

title: Pay-Per-Decibel Neighbor Trust for Data Centers
one_liner: An independent trust that owns a sensor mesh around a data center and automatically pays nearby households every time the hum exceeds agreed limits, turning 'trust us' into a self-executing contract.
customer: Data center developers and hyperscaler community-affairs teams, their land-use counsel, and counties negotiating community benefit agreements. Pre-application projects facing a rezoning fight are the entry point.
problem: Local opposition blocked or delayed roughly $130B of US data center projects in 2026, and opposition groups more than doubled to 833 by March. Developers' flat checks get called bribes: a $10,000-per-household offer to 4,500 households was rejected by residents in September. Noise promises are unenforceable, and dBA ordinances miss the low-frequency hum residents complain about. Counties lack staff to monitor compliance.
solution: A neighbor trust, funded by a developer bond, with three parts. (1) Trust-owned acoustic, low-frequency and vibration sensors, publicly viewable in real time. (2) A pre-agreed parametric schedule: any household within the radius gets an automatic payment for each night the level exceeds the threshold, so the payout works like a warranty on quiet. (3) Escalation funding for window and HVAC retrofits if exceedances persist. The trust also reports compliance to the county, giving regulators enforcement without new staff.
why_now: Opposition is peaking (about 120 projects stalled in H1 2026, more than 300 state bills, moratoria such as New York's), and developers are now experimenting with direct household payments and getting burned on credibility. Developers now need a neutral administrator, and no obvious specialist exists.
revenue_model: Developer pays $150k to $500k setup per campus, plus 8% to 12% of the annual fund as administration, plus sensor-as-a-service fees. Add county compliance-monitoring contracts. A single multi-billion-dollar campus can absorb this as a rounding error against months of delay.
non_obvious_insight: Neighbors rarely reject data centers over money. They reject unmeasured, unpriced harm. Making the harm measured and self-paying changes the negotiation and gives the developer a real financial reason to buy quieter chillers and dampers. The low-frequency, night-time signature is what the trust measures, and ordinances miss it.
first_30_days: List the next five county hearings on data center rezoning from local news and Data Center Watch. Hire a freelance acoustic engineer and build a $2k-per-node sensor kit from off-the-shelf parts. Offer a free 60-day neutral baseline noise map to one pending project, in front of both the developer and the opposition group. Convert that goodwill into a paid pre-application baseline of $50k to $100k and an MOU for the trust structure.

title: Agent-Buyable Assay Storefronts With QC-Gated Escrow
angle: Pairing 1: AI agents & agent economy x Biotech tools / synbio / lab automation
one_liner: Turn idle university cores and orphaned biotech labs into machine-buyable assay shops where payment releases automatically only if the raw instrument data passes pre-agreed control checks.
customer: Sellers are university core facilities, small CROs and shuttered-biotech labs with idle instruments. Buyers are protein-design, synbio and 'AI scientist' teams whose agents generate thousands of candidates. Revenue comes from a take rate on transactions.
problem: Design-build-test is now bounded by assays, not DNA (the Weizmann 2.5 billion antibody fragments cost only EUR 38,000 in DNA synthesis). Yet bench services are sold by 'request a quote' forms and PDF emails that agents cannot use, and buyers cannot judge whether a result is real. NIH turbulence (grant caps, K99 restrictions, staff protections stripped) and biotech layoffs (15,000+ cuts) leave cores and dead-company labs with idle capacity and no sales function. Agent commerce already shows the pattern: RentAHuman had about 590,000 sign-ups against about 11,300 bounties, so supply is abundant and trusted demand is scarce.
solution: Each standardized assay (BLI/SPR binding, thermal shift, expression titer, mycoplasma test, mass-spec ID, sequencing verification) becomes an MCP or ACP offer with price, turnaround, sample requirements, shipping label and acceptance criteria. Money sits in escrow and releases when deterministic rules on the raw output pass (positive/negative control window, Z' above a threshold, expected ladder). A failure triggers an automatic rerun or refund, so no one argues about disputes.
why_now: Machine-payment rails shipped in 2026 (Stripe/Tempo MPP on March 18, x402 to the Linux Foundation in April, ACP/AP2). Frontier labs are running hundreds of parallel bio-agents. NIH funding instability is pushing cores to seek outside revenue, and biotech distress in 2026 is creating idle labs.
revenue_model: 5-10% take rate on assay orders, float and expedite fees on escrow, listing setup fees for sellers ($500-2,000), and a managed-account tier for large protein-design teams.
non_obvious_insight: The unsolved dispute problem in agentic commerce becomes tractable for physical science because instruments emit machine-checkable controls. Acceptance tests on raw files stand in for human judgment, and academic core capacity is the cheapest, most trustworthy supply pool exactly when NIH money is shaky.
first_30_days: Sign 5 cores (mass spec, BLI, sequencing, flow) and list 10 SKUs with fixed prices. Run everything semi-manually behind a simple API and Stripe. Offer $2K free-assay bounties to 10 protein-design groups (BindCraft/RFdiffusion users) and have their scripts place orders. Publish pass rates and turnaround. Charge 8% from day one.

title: Data Center Deal Desk for Rural Counties
one_liner: An independent negotiating desk that gives county and township boards a benchmark of every comparable data-center abatement and community-benefit contract, a counter term sheet and a fiscal model, paid for by the developer's review escrow.
customer: County commissions, township boards, school boards and local economic-development authorities facing data-center proposals, plus state associations of counties and resident coalitions.
problem: Developers have negotiated dozens of deals and arrive with NDAs and shell LLCs. Counties have negotiated none, and commissioners vote on abatements they can't benchmark. Leverage disappears once approvals are granted. Terms on water use, noise, diesel backup hours, decommissioning bonds, grid-cost protection and clawbacks vary wildly.
solution: Parse every signed abatement, PILOT, host-community and large-load utility agreement obtainable (the Federation of American Scientists started collecting signed agreements in early 2026, and public records requests fill gaps) into a comparable clause database. Deliver a two-week Deal Review: where each term falls against the median and best deals, a counter term sheet, fiscal, water and power impact modeling, and a 'second chair' during meetings. Fees are typically recoverable from the applicant through a third-party review escrow.
why_now: The 2026 data-center land rush has local governments scrambling: most local ordinances and ballot measures tracked in 2026 passed, many deals sit behind NDAs, and counties from Texas to Ohio are tabling or denying abatements while others approve blind. LLMs make reading hundreds of messy contracts cheap. Incumbent consultants and county attorneys don't have a comparables dataset.
revenue_model: $12k to $40k per deal review (billed to the developer's review escrow where the county allows it), annual data license for state county associations ($30k to $100k) and, later, a pre-vetted 'fast-lane' term sheet that developers pay to use.
non_obvious_insight: Information asymmetry, not law, is the county's problem, and the cheapest fix is a set of comparables. Commissioners also fear being first or being fleeced, so 'we asked for what the median county got' gives political cover. Charging the applicant through the review escrow means the buyer, a cash-strapped county, doesn't need a budget line.
first_30_days: Collect 100 signed agreements from the FAS repository, Texas Chapter 312 filings and records requests, and code them into a comparison table. Publish free state scorecards. Email commissioners in counties with pending abatement votes and offer a $5k rapid clause redline, asking the county to request that the developer pay under its review-fee ordinance.

title: Turn Podcast Fans Into Local Chapters
one_liner: A chapter-in-a-box that lets mid-size creators convert engaged, lonely audiences into weekly local meetups, with insurance, host training and venues handled.
customer: Superfans aged 18-34 paying about $12 a month for a local chapter. Creators with 50k-1M followers are the distribution partners on a revenue share. Brand sponsors pay for chapter access.
problem: Insiders treat parasocial attachment as a symptom of loneliness. But an audience with a shared in-group reference is already a pre-formed community, and creators' inboxes are full of 'is there a meetup in my city?' Creators cannot run 40 city chapters themselves because of liability, hosting, venues and safety. Discord and online-only communities do not fix in-person isolation.
solution: The platform reads audience data to find the top 10 fan-dense cities per creator. It recruits and trains volunteer hosts from top fans, provides liability insurance, a code of conduct and venue partnerships (breweries, cafes), and delivers a monthly 'creator drop' built for group listening or viewing. Each chapter runs weekly or biweekly with a 30-40 member target.
why_now: Fan-led IRL groups (run clubs, book clubs, hobby meetups) exploded through 2024-25. Feed fatigue and AI-slop backlash push young adults toward real-world belonging. Creators need revenue beyond volatile ad and sponsor income, and Meetup's post-acquisition policy troubles have left organizers looking for alternatives.
revenue_model: 20-25% of chapter dues, venue referral fees and sponsor packages. A 40-member chapter at $12 a month is $480 a month. Creators keep about 40% of dues.
non_obvious_insight: Parasocial is not the disease, it is the on-ramp. The cheapest cold start for local community is an audience that already shares references. What is missing is boring, outsourceable logistics and risk management.
first_30_days: Sign 3 niche-hobby creators with 100-300k audiences. Use their email or Patreon ZIP-code data to pick one city each. Recruit hosts from their Discords. Run the first brewery meetups and charge $12 a month from day one, aiming for 30 members per chapter.

title: Farm-to-Factory Water Supply Assurance
angle: Pairing 2: Manufacturing reshoring/tariffs x Water infrastructure
one_liner: A diligence-plus-settlement service that sells expanding plants a permit-grade, verified acre-foot supply by leasing fallowed farm water in drought-stressed Western basins.
customer: Plant developers, site-selection teams and economic-development agencies for semiconductor, pharma and food plants in AZ, TX, ID and UT. Irrigation districts and farmers are the supply side.
problem: Water is now a siting gate: Texas froze grid connections over water, the Colorado River's 2027-2036 framework forces farm cuts, and Amazon put $20M into farm conservation with no settlement layer. Factories need a legally defensible supply and 'water neutral' commitments, and farmers cannot easily sell verified savings.
solution: Start with a $15-40k water-supply diligence report (rights, drought exposure, discharge capacity, PFAS in source). Then structure and meter option-style leases with farmers, with satellite and meter verification, and issue an assurance letter usable in permitting.
why_now: The Aug 2026 Colorado River Record of Decision, 49.6% of the US in drought, and reshoring in water-intensive sectors (electronics +35%, pharma +32%, food +17% in robot orders) collide.
revenue_model: Diligence fee plus 5-8% of lease flow and a verification fee per acre-foot.
non_obvious_insight: The cheapest new industrial water supply is a farmer's fallowed field, but only if someone provides the paperwork that turns it into a permit-grade asset.
first_30_days: Pick one county (for example Pinal, AZ). Sign three farmers on non-binding option terms. Sell two diligence reports to plant real-estate teams or EDCs, and recruit a water-rights attorney as an advisor.

title: Book-Not-Shop Roll-Up of Retiring Machine Shops
one_liner: Buy retiring shops' customer books, programs and drawings on earn-outs, then migrate the work to a partner network.
customer: Owners of 5-40 person machine shops aged 60+ who want a clean exit. The buyer's customers keep their supply.
problem: About 60% of US manufacturing firms have owners aged 55+, about 150k small and mid-size firms are near retirement, and customers often leave when the owner retires (per American Machinist and MMS). MMS admits no dataset exists. Existing buyers such as Compass Precision buy whole shops with real estate, iron and payroll, which is capital-heavy and risky.
solution: Buy only the customer relationships, drawings, programs, fixtures and quality records for about 1-1.5x annual gross profit, paid mostly as an earn-out on retained revenue over 24-36 months. The owner runs a transition site for 6-12 months. Work then moves to 3-5 partner shops that have spare capacity. Equipment is auctioned or leased. AI digitizes quote history and setup sheets.
why_now: The retirement wave is under way and PMI at 55.6 (highest since May 2022) keeps demand steady. PE roll-ups have proven that a market exists, and a capital-light structure fits smaller teams.
revenue_model: 15-25% gross margin on migrated work. Slotting fees from partner shops. Deal capital is $250-750k per deal, mostly as earn-out.
non_obvious_insight: The asset is customer trust and tacit programs, not buildings or machines. An earn-out tied to retained revenue makes both sides fight the main failure mode of roll-ups, which is customer attrition.
first_30_days: Build a list of 300 target shops from state registries, LinkedIn and outreach. Sign three LOIs on owner-friendly terms. Line up three partner shops with capacity. Raise a $1M search-fund-style pool or use SBA financing.

title: Consumer-Side Debt Negotiation Agent for Brazil
one_liner: A WhatsApp agent that reads a household's Open Finance data and negotiates all its debts on the debtor's behalf.
customer: Over-indebted Brazilian households, paying a success fee.
problem: Household debt is around 82% by the cited indicator, delinquency is at a record, and Lula's Sep 25 relief may reach under 1% of defaults. People face many creditors and rarely know discounts are available.
solution: With consent, pull debts from Open Finance, build a repayment plan, negotiate through lender collection channels and debt portals, and set up Pix Automatico debits. The wedge is revolving card debt and overdraft for low-income users.
why_now: Open Finance and Pix Automatico are mature and LLM agents can now negotiate reliably. The online betting ban leaves ex-bettors with debts and no plan.
revenue_model: 10-15% of the discount obtained, charged only on success.
non_obvious_insight: Existing collections platforms are lender-paid and optimise recovery. A debtor-side agent exposes rate arbitrage and gives lenders a rational counterparty at scale.
first_30_days: Run a concierge pilot with 100 users, using humans plus AI drafting, to learn discount rates by lender. Check consumer-protection rules first.

title: Book the Unbookable: Agents for Offline Suppliers
one_liner: A voice-and-WhatsApp agent phones, negotiates and confirms bookings with small inns, guides and boat operators that have no API, then turns each one into bookable inventory.
customer: Independent travel advisors and small DMCs first, later AI trip-planning apps and OTAs seeking long-tail inventory.
problem: The best small inns, agriturismi, ryokan, guides and boat operators take bookings by phone, WhatsApp or email in local languages, with deposits by bank transfer. Advisors spend hours per booking, AI agents cannot book them and OTAs do not list them. Hotel-side voice AI is crowded (for example Dextr AI's seed), but buyer-side is empty.
solution: A real-time multilingual voice and text agent calls or messages the supplier, checks availability, negotiates a net rate within the advisor's limits and sends the deposit. A human verifies the money step. Every completed booking builds a structured supplier profile (hours, languages, deposit rules) that becomes API-bookable next time.
why_now: Real-time voice models now handle 30+ languages, WhatsApp Business is universal, and agentic payment tooling exists. Shrinking booking lead times and rerouted travel create demand for fast alternatives beyond OTA inventory.
revenue_model: USD 20-60 or 3-5% of booking value per booking from advisors, SaaS for DMCs, and later a take rate from suppliers and inventory data licensing.
non_obvious_insight: Long-tail supply is invisible to agents because it lacks an API, not because it lacks quality. The cheapest API is a phone call made by a machine with a human closing the money step, and each call builds an inventory graph nobody owns.
first_30_days: Pick Japan, Italy and Greece. Recruit 15 independent travel advisors and process 100 bookings semi-manually with human voice operators shadowing the agent at USD 30 per booking. Measure time saved and conversion.

title: A Teaching Hospital Inside a Dead Hospital
one_liner: Lease a wing of a closed hospital and run it as a full-scale simulation hospital that nursing schools rent by the student-day.
customer: Community-college ADN and BSN programs turning away applicants, state workforce boards, and health systems that want a new-grad pipeline.
problem: Nursing schools turned away a record 93,176 qualified applications in 2025 (AACN, May 2026). The binding constraint is clinical placement sites, plus faculty vacancies above 7%. Many state boards allow up to 50% of clinical hours in high-fidelity simulation, but most school sim labs are a few beds in a converted classroom. Medicaid cuts are pushing more rural hospitals to close.
solution: Lease a closed hospital floor that already has medical gas, patient rooms, nurse stations, ICU bays and an OR. Fill it with liquidation beds and mannequins. Staff it with simulation faculty and local standardized patients such as retirees and theater students. Run immersive multi-day, 12-hour shift simulations from admission to discharge, sold per student-day or by semester cohort. Design to NCSBN and INACSL standards and get state board sign-off.
why_now: The record turned-away numbers landed in May 2026. 38 state boards had specific simulation rules by 2021 and more have followed. Rural closures are rising with the 2025 federal Medicaid cuts, so vacant, fully plumbed buildings are appearing cheaply. The $10B/yr Rural Health Transformation funds (FY26-30) create state workforce money to pay for seats.
revenue_model: $150-300 per student-day, or cohort contracts of $40-120k per semester per program. Health-system sponsorship for pipeline seats. Workforce and state grant funding.
non_obvious_insight: Simulation labs fail from unrealistic space and thin faculty, not from a lack of mannequins, and a dead hospital is the only building that already is the environment, priced at less than replacement cost. The buyer is a school with a waitlist, backed by employers and state money that want more graduates.
first_30_days: Pick two states with permissive simulation rules and long nursing waitlists. Call ADN program directors at 10 community colleges and offer a paid 2-day 'shift-in-a-day' pilot. Identify 3 closed hospitals through state health-department lists. Recruit a retired nurse educator as clinical lead, rent mannequins for a pilot, and charge $12-20k per cohort.

title: Outpatient Parvo Kits for Shelters and Low-Cost Clinics
one_liner: Parvo is treated as inpatient-only, but a standardized ambulatory protocol in a box plus remote nurse monitoring can cut cost per case dramatically for shelters that otherwise euthanize.
customer: Municipal animal services, shelters and spay-neuter/low-cost clinics. Secondary: urgent-care clinics serving low-income clients.
problem: Inpatient parvo care often costs thousands of dollars, so shelters and owners choose euthanasia, and vets suffer moral distress. The briefing notes vet care is nearly half of pet-cost inflation since 2019 and that clinicians routinely alter plans for money. The outpatient protocols exist (Colorado State published one in 2017 reporting survival in the range of hospitalization; re-verify in the pilot) but only as PDFs, not as a product with logistics.
solution: A vet-signed kit per case (SC fluids, maropitant, antibiotics, syringes, nutrition support, dosing cards, video training) sold by a partner clinic-of-record. Twice-daily photo/video/weight/hydration logs are reviewed by an RVT desk with DVM sign-off, with hard escalation rules to inpatient transfer. A shared outcome registry proves results to funders. Extend to other ambulatory-able acute problems (uncomplicated gastroenteritis, SC-fluid CKD cats).
why_now: Access philanthropy just scaled (Duffield 2026-09-17; PetSmart Charities), and funders want cost-per-outcome evidence. Shelters are overcrowded and Texas transports have been slowed by screwworm restrictions. Remote VCPR rules are loosening piecemeal, and spectrum-of-care thinking is now mainstream.
revenue_model: $150-300 per case for kit plus monitoring, versus thousands for inpatient care. Annual shelter subscription ($2-5K) with usage tiers, often paid from grant dollars. Protocol licensing to low-cost clinic chains.
non_obvious_insight: The 'standard of care' for parvo is partly a business-model artifact: hospitals are paid to hospitalize. Nobody sells the cheaper protocol as a logistics-and-monitoring product, and the buyers (shelters, funders) are motivated by lives saved per dollar.
first_30_days: Partner with 3 shelters and one shelter-medicine vet. Assemble kits from wholesale distributors via the vet's prescriptions. Run 20 cases with structured data on survival, days to eating and cost. Apply for a $10K micro-grant to underwrite the pilot. Publish a one-page outcomes summary.

title: Night Ledger: Sleep Evidence for Live-In Aides
one_liner: A camera-free $35 bedroom-door sensor kit that logs every night-time awakening of a dementia patient, giving live-in agencies court-grade proof of sleep or interruption, and a case for the second aide.
customer: Licensed home care agencies with 20-300 24-hour live-in cases, starting with Medicaid-contracted agencies in NYC, Long Island, Westchester and northern NJ. Secondary: families who employ live-in aides directly. Agencies pay.
problem: Live-in aides are paid for 13 of 24 hours. That is legal in New York only if the aide gets 8 hours of sleep, 5 of them uninterrupted, plus 3 hours for meals. A dementia patient who sundowns, wanders and needs toileting at 2am makes that fiction. The only evidence of sleep is the aide's own signed timesheet. Agencies face wage class actions and NYSDOL claims. Aides are underpaid and quit. The night, the most expensive and dangerous stretch of care, is the least measured.
solution: Two or three battery-powered motion or mmWave sensors (bedroom door, hallway, bathroom, exit door) and a hub that phones home. There is no video and no audio, because aides hate being watched and families in some states cannot legally record them. Each morning it produces a one-page Night Report: the longest uninterrupted stretch, the number of get-ups, exit-seeking events, and a one-tap aide confirmation of what was actually done. Quiet nights support the 13-hour pay. Noisy nights trigger a pay correction and build a documented case for the plan to authorize split-shift (two-aide) coverage. Families get 2am exit-seeking alerts on the same hardware.
why_now: In January 2026 a New York court reopened hundreds of shelved 24-hour-aide wage claims against NYSDOL and granted class certification (Legal Aid and NCLEJ). Federal DOL has only proposed reinstating the companionship exemption (July 2025). The 2013 rule is still the law, private rights of action are untouched, and state law in NY, NJ and CA applies regardless. Sensors, BLE and mmWave chips are now cheap enough to rent per case. The oldest boomers turn 80 this year, so live-in dementia cases are growing.
revenue_model: $79 per active live-in case per month, with the sensor kit rented and shipped. A one-time $1,500 to $3,000 wage-liability audit for agencies is the entry product. Families add-on at $29 per month for night alerts. Later, a fee for documentation packages that support split-shift authorization requests.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone treats the 13-hour rule as a labor-cost fight. Insiders know the same nightly record is a liability shield for the agency, proof of a heavier case that can justify two aides billed at full rate, and evidence for the aide, all at once. Nobody has built it because the buyer, the agency, has spent years preferring not to have the data. A class action changes that preference. Cameras are the wrong tool. Aides quit over them, and door-and-hallway motion data is enough.
first_30_days: Buy 40 off-the-shelf Zigbee or BLE motion sensors and a Pi or cellular hub. Write a script that emails a Night Report. Sell the audit as a service to 3 small LHCSAs in Brooklyn, Queens or Bergen County through wage-and-hour defense attorneys and home care association meetings, by offering a free 2-week pilot on their five heaviest cases. Ask two worker centers to beta test with aides and give aides their own copy of the log. The first paid pilots should come from agencies that were just sued or received a DOL inquiry.

title: Facility-Clearance-in-a-Box and Cleared Bench
one_liner: A facility-clearance sponsor plus a rentable bench of already-cleared engineers for the wave of newly funded defense startups winning first classified subcontracts.
customer: Series A-C defense startups and small business subcontractors with a first classified task order but no facility clearance or cleared staff.
problem: Defense startups raised $14.6B in five months of 2026, and awards are accelerating. Startups cannot sponsor clearances without a contract and cannot start work without cleared people. Sponsorship and adjudication take months, so classified work stalls and startups lose the window.
solution: A cleared small business holds the FCL and employs a bench of cleared engineers, program managers and security officers. It subcontracts them to startups by the hour, provides FSO services, and manages the startup's own path to clearance. Includes shared SCIF time at partner facilities.
why_now: Record capital plus fast-lane vehicles (Megatron IDIQ, the Space Force valley-of-death office, Navy marketplaces) create hundreds of first-time classified subcontractors at once. Federal staff shortages mean primes want ready capacity.
revenue_model: Cleared-labor margin (25-40% on $150-250 per hour), monthly FSO retainers ($4-10K), and SCIF seat fees. A roll-up of small cleared staffing shops adds scale.
non_obvious_insight: Cash is no longer scarce for defense startups, but time-to-cleared-work is. The binding constraint has moved from funding to a slow, government-controlled credential that can be rented.
first_30_days: Acquire or partner with a small cleared firm that already holds an FCL. Recruit 5-8 cleared freelancers and retired government staff. Pitch the 20 most recently funded startups and place the first two engineers.

title: Service-Linked Loans for Vet Students Facing Caps
one_liner: Grad PLUS ended for new borrowers on July 1, 2026, and vet school now hits a $50K-per-year, $200K aggregate federal cap; clinics and rural practices can fill the gap with work-linked financing that doubles as retention.
customer: First- and second-year DVM students at high-cost programs (borrowers), and clinic groups, rural food-animal practices and state programs (employers who fund the retention hook).
problem: Veterinary medicine is one of 11 professional programs under the new caps, and out-of-state or private DVM costs can exceed $200K over four years, so students will lean on pricier private loans or cosigners. Meanwhile employers pay sign-on bonuses with no retention hook, and rural and food-animal practices cannot recruit; only 1.3% of vets are in food-animal practice, and South Texas is under strain from screwworm.
solution: A gap-financing product where employers pre-commit to fund a student's tuition gap in exchange for a 3-5 year service commitment with vesting forgiveness (like health-service scholarships). We underwrite, originate through a bank or CDFI partner, and administer vesting, recourse and state-incentive stacking, including Texas' funded rural veterinary incentive program.
why_now: The first cohort under the caps is enrolling this fall. Roll-ups are hungry for associates, Texas has funded rural vet incentives, and screwworm has made food-animal vet scarcity visible to policymakers.
revenue_model: 1-2% origination plus an annual administration fee paid by employers (8-12% of loan balance vested), and a spread on the loan book.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders see loan caps as a schools' problem. The second-order effect is that caps create a class of employers willing to pay to lock scarce DVMs four years early, turning tuition into the cheapest recruiting channel the industry has had.
first_30_days: Interview financial-aid officers at 4 high-cost schools. Sign term sheets with 3 employers (a rural practice group, a regional corporate group, a state program). Line up one bank or CDFI partner and get legal review on income-share and recourse rules in 3 states. Pilot with 10 students.

title: Voice-Clone-Proof Verbal Deals for Grain and Cattle
angle: Pairing 2: Food & agriculture x Cybersecurity/deepfake fraud/identity verification/scams
one_liner: A two-channel confirmation step and verified-payee ledger that makes phone-and-handshake commodity deals safe from cloned voices and redirected payments.
customer: Regional grain elevators and co-ops, livestock auction markets and order buyers, ag input retailers, and the ag lenders that finance them.
problem: Agriculture runs on calls: bids, forward contracts, cattle sales, input prepays and cash rents, with confirmation by email. About 3 seconds of audio can clone a farmer's or merchandiser's voice, and BEC cost $3.05B in 2025. Retail beef hit a record $9.64/lb, contract sizes are up, and farm distress attracts fake-buyer scams. Small operations have no fraud team, and cross-bank recovery through the FBI's process is rarely accessible to them.
solution: Verify each farmer's bank account ownership once, with a passphrase or app approval. Any verbal contract above a threshold, or any change of payee, triggers an out-of-band push approval or a callback to a pre-registered number. Settlement pays only to verified accounts. Integrate with grain accounting and auction-clerk systems. Extend to cash-rent payments to older landlords and to the December input prepay season.
why_now: Voice cloning is mainstream. Chainalysis reports impersonation scams up 1,400% with average payments up 253%, and the FBI's Sept 17 2026 PSA cites AI video calls in law-enforcement impersonation. The December prepay season is about ten weeks away, and record livestock prices raise the stakes.
revenue_model: $300-800 a month per elevator or auction location plus $0.50-2 per verified payment. Lenders pay per portfolio, and cyber insurers may give premium credits.
non_obvious_insight: In agriculture the voice is the credential. Forty-year relationships mean nobody asks for ID, and voice cloning breaks the oldest trust protocol in commodity trading. The paying customer is the elevator or auction, which bears misdirected settlements, not the farmer. The tool plugs into settlement systems that banks cannot see.
first_30_days: Interview 20 elevator merchandisers and controllers. Pilot with 2 regional co-ops during harvest settlements using a bank account-owner check plus text push approval. Present to auction-market clerk groups. Ask a cyber-insurance broker about premium credits. Offer a December prepay fraud drill.

title: Fractional Licensed Qualifier for Trade-Business Buyers
one_liner: Rent a vetted master-licensed professional as the bona fide qualifying officer, so first-time buyers of HVAC, plumbing, electrical and engineering firms can get financed and keep the license alive after the seller leaves.
customer: First-time acquirers (search funders, SBA-financed individual buyers, independent sponsors, small holdcos) of licensed-trade companies with $1-15M revenue. The buyer pays monthly. SBA lenders and business brokers are the referral channel.
problem: In licensed trades the license and credentials are the real asset, and they walk out the door with the seller at closing. Buyers without a license get rejected by banks, and a replacement certification takes 6-12 months. Search-fund and ETA (entrepreneurship through acquisition) volume is at record levels, so more non-credentialed buyers are chasing these businesses.
solution: A bench of retired or semi-retired license holders (master plumbers, electrical contractors, PEs, inspectors, HVAC qualifiers). Each is placed as a bona fide officer or employee under a state-specific structure with real supervisory duties, E&O cover and indemnity. The service comes with (1) a lender-ready 'credential continuity package' (letter, duties, key-person plan), (2) a 12-month program that sponsors an internal successor through exams and hours, and (3) a state-by-state compliance library. It operates only in states where counsel confirms the qualifier rules allow this. License-lending schemes are illegal in many states, so compliance is the moat.
why_now: About 100 new US/Canadian search funds launched in 2023 (record), and acquisition volume grew from $110M to $880M per Stanford data summarized on Wikipedia. More than half of US small-business owners are 55+ without succession plans. PE Hub's September 2026 feed shows continuing PE appetite for HVAC, pest control and vet add-ons, which lifts what owners of licensed businesses expect to be paid and pulls more of them into sale processes. Buyer supply now exceeds credentialed-buyer supply.
revenue_model: $2-4K/month retainer per placement for 12-24 months. $1.5-2.5K one-time lender package. Sponsored successor-certification program billed at cost plus margin. Later, group E&O and key-person insurance placement commissions.
non_obvious_insight: The binding constraint in trades acquisitions is the credential, not capital or price. Jack Rauch's Tew & Taylor deal was rejected by multiple banks because he had no building-code license or experience. Their words: 'you don't have this license, you don't have this experience... good luck. We won't touch it.' He had to close on family-office debt at a 33/33/33 cap table (https://www.acquiringminds.co/articles/jack-rauch-tew-taylor). Manolo Diaz Corrada's Bonneville deal names certifications as a single point of failure that take 'six months to a year to acquire' and are not economical to duplicate (https://www.acquiringminds.co/articles/manolo-diaz-corrada-bonneville-group). Nobody sells credential continuity as a product. Brokers treat it as the buyer's problem, and lenders treat it as a deal-killer. Caveat: the evidence is operator interviews with a small sample, and the legal structure must be validated state by state.
first_30_days: Pick two states with well-documented qualifier rules (for example FL and TX) and pay for a counsel memo on each. Recruit 10 retired license holders through trade associations, retiree groups and union alumni networks. Build a one-page lender-facing continuity plan and show it to 10-15 SBA lenders and 20 business brokers. Post the offer in ETA communities (Searchfunder, Acquiring Minds audience) and sign 2-3 buyers with signed LOIs for paid pilot placements at a discount in exchange for case studies.

title: Dog Walk Plus: Wellness Checks for Isolated Seniors
one_liner: Turn the daily dog walk at an older client's home into a consented, structured wellness check with escalation, sold to their adult children.
customer: Adult children of independent-living parents who own dogs and live alone (the payer). Later: geriatric care managers, home health agencies, senior housing operators, and long-term care insurers.
problem: A dog walker is the only outsider who enters an older person's home every day at a predictable hour. I have found clients on the floor, and noticed early cognitive decline: the dog fed twice or not at all, pills left out, mail piling up, new bruises. Adult children call and ask us informally, we have no protocol, no consent, and no escalation ladder. Seniors refuse pendants and sensors but accept a walker, because it is about the dog and their dignity stays intact. The dog is also why many seniors delay going to the ER.
solution: A 'Walk Plus' plan built on a written consent from the senior. Alongside the walk, the walker does a 60-second structured check (a 10-tap list covering mobility, orientation, medications visible, food in the fridge, home temperature, bruises, mood, dog condition). Family gets a weekly text summary with trend flags. There is a clear escalation ladder (no answer at the door, then family call, then agreed non-emergency welfare check), and a pet emergency plan with keys and authority on file so that if the owner is hospitalized the walker becomes the dog's custodian. That prevents surrenders and removes the reason to refuse the hospital.
why_now: A large cohort is turning 65 and aging in place, home-care aide capacity is tight, and adult children are stretched thin as remote caregivers. Structured notes are now easy to summarize into a plain-language weekly update. Health plans and senior-service providers are looking for cheap ways to catch problems early, and a daily reason to enter the home is exactly what monitoring products lack.
revenue_model: Walks at $25 to $45 per visit plus a $29 to $49 monthly check-in fee paid by the family. B2B later: license the protocol and reporting to home health agencies and senior housing operators, and sell trend data (with consent) to long-term care insurers or aging-in-place programs.
non_obvious_insight: The dog is the Trojan horse that makes monitoring acceptable. A pendant says 'you're frail'; a dog walker says 'I'm here for the dog.' Walkers already do this informally and unpaid, so the product is less a new service than a protocol, a consent form, and an escalation path around something that already happens every day.
first_30_days: Convert existing senior clients (most walkers have three to six) with a one-page consent form. Build the check-in with a form and Twilio text summaries, no app needed. Partner with two local geriatric care managers who charge by the hour for the same visibility, and post in senior center and church newsletters. Target 10 paying families and track escalations as your proof.

title: Robot-Training Disassembly Lab for E-Scrap Magnets
angle: Pairing 1: AI labor-market disruption x waste/circular economy/critical minerals
one_liner: A small teardown shop where displaced office workers are paid to take apart hard drives and servers on camera, so sales of robot-training data cover the labor that makes rare-earth magnet recovery uneconomic.
customer: Two paying buyers. (1) Physical-AI and robotics labs that need real contact-rich manipulation data. (2) Rare-earth processors and ITAD firms that want magnets and boards already pulled out of steel and PCB streams. The workers are laid-off office staff and underemployed recent grads.
problem: The circular-materials brief says the rare-earth bottleneck is collection and disassembly, not chemistry, and that pulling magnets from hard drives often costs more than the magnets are worth. Robotics labs are short of messy, real-world demonstration data. Meanwhile the expert-gig data economy (Mercor and similar) pays only for screen work, contractors complain of falling pay, and recent-grad underemployment is 42%.
solution: Rent a bay near an ITAD or data-center decommissioner and take in drives and servers that are already sanitized under NIST 800-88. Workers wear head cameras and instrumented gloves or tool sensors and follow step protocols. An annotation pipeline labels screw types, connectors and failure cases. Sell the licensed video and force data by the annotated hour. Sell the pre-extracted magnet fractions, aluminum and boards to processors. Later, the same corpus trains a disassembly arm that lowers labor cost. Workers earn wages plus a skills log.
why_now: Physical-AI funding and data hunger are at a peak in 2026. DoD and DOE are subsidizing domestic rare-earth supply, and hyperscalers are pushing processors to recover magnets. DRAM prices are up about 400% since early 2024, and data centers turn hardware over every 12-18 months, so teardown yield keeps rising. White-collar hiring is frozen for the young (Stanford: 22-25-year-olds in AI-exposed jobs are 19% below trend).
revenue_model: Data licensing per annotated hour (hypothesis to test: $35-60/hr, versus roughly $25-28/hr loaded labor). Materials sales of magnets, aluminum, boards and DRAM/SSD. Per-unit processing fees from ITAD partners. Later, licensing the teardown protocols and a robot-ready dataset.
non_obvious_insight: Disassembly looks unprofitable only because we value just the recovered material. The task has a second output, training data, that has no recovery-cost floor. The uglier and more variable the end-of-life product, the more out-of-distribution and valuable the data is to robotics labs. Recycling's mess is the data moat, and the displaced labor is the cheap input.
first_30_days: Sign one ITAD or decommissioner for a free lot of about 500 sanitized drives. Sign one robotics team for a paid 100-hour pilot. Recruit six workers from laid-off tech and helpdesk groups. Build three capture stations (camera plus glove rig, about $1.5K each). Sell the first magnet and aluminum lot to a local processor to prove the unit economics.

title: Court-Rules MCP Server With a Deadline Warranty
one_liner: Effective-dated, human-verified court rules, judge standing orders and deadline math for one state at a time, exposed to any AI agent, with fee credits if a computed deadline is wrong.
customer: Solo and small firms (5 or fewer attorneys) in personal injury, family, criminal defense and landlord-tenant who already run Clio or MyCase and are starting to use Claude or ChatGPT agents. Later, legal-AI vendors that buy the rule set by API.
problem: Missed deadlines are among the most common malpractice claims (background knowledge, verify). General models know case law roughly but not this county's local rules, this judge's standing order (including AI-use certifications), or this year's fee schedule. The rules live as PDFs across thousands of court sites and change constantly, and big-firm docketing systems are priced and built for large firms.
solution: Start with one state pack, for example Texas civil. It holds statutes of limitation, civil procedure, local rules of the top counties and judge standing orders, each effective-dated with a hashed source PDF. MCP tools such as compute_deadline(event, court, date) and check_filing(court, judge, doc_type) return the date, the rule cites and a confidence flag. A deterministic engine does the date math (no LLM arithmetic), paid legal editors verify the high-use rules, and change alerts go out. A small warranty (fee credit plus capped reimbursement) backs the deadline output.
why_now: 8am's MyCase says 60+ firms, mostly 5 or fewer attorneys, adopted its Claude MCP connector (73 actions) in the first month, so small firms are now consuming practice tools through agents. Case law is open and the model is free, but local procedure is not in any frontier legal product.
revenue_model: $79-149/month per firm per state pack, an API license of $2-10k/month for legal-AI vendors, and a premium warranty tier.
non_obvious_insight: When the model is free and the corpus is open, the scarce asset is authoritative, effective-dated local procedure with a liability wrapper. Nobody can warrant an LLM's legal reasoning, but a rules engine plus editorial verification is exactly where a warranty is underwritable.
first_30_days: Pick one state and one practice area. Hand-build the 300 highest-frequency rules with two contract paralegals (about $8-10k), ship a free MCP server, and recruit 15 firms through a state solo and small-firm bar list. Charge $99/month after the trial, publish an accuracy audit, and keep the warranty to a $500 credit until loss data exists.
